entries.95c019fca581f107989513da71e6afc862b69adb: <div sID="gen11680" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="69" osisID="Ps.69" sID="Ps.69"/> <div eID="gen11680" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11681" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen11682" type="x-p"/> David penned this psalm when he was in affliction; and in it, I. He complains of the great distress and trouble he was in and earnestly begs of God to relieve and succour him, <reference osisRef="Ps.69.1-Ps.69.21">ver. 1-21</reference>. II. He imprecates the judgments of God upon his persecutors, <reference osisRef="Ps.69.22-Ps.69.29">ver. 22-29</reference>. III. He concludes with the voice of joy and praise, in an assurance that God would help and succour him, and would do well for the church, <reference osisRef="Ps.69.30-Ps.69.36">ver. 30-36</reference>. Now, in this, David was a type of Christ, and divers passages in this psalm are applied to Christ in the new Testament and are said to have their accomplishment in him (<reference osisRef="Ps.69.4">ver. 4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.69.9">9</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.69.21">21</reference>), and <reference osisRef="Ps.69.22">ver. 22</reference> refers to the enemies of Christ. So that (like the <reference osisRef="Ps.22.1-Ps.22.31">twenty-second psalm</reference>) it begins with the humiliation and ends with the exaltation of Christ, one branch of which was the destruction of the Jewish nation for persecuting him, which the imprecations here are predictions of. In singing this psalm we must have an eye to the sufferings of Christ, and the glory that followed, not forgetting the sufferings of Christians too, and the glory that shall follow them; for it may lead us to think of the ruin reserved for the persecutors and the rest reserved for the persecuted.
entries.aeb2b72f33e9e6eaf86c54d1cc081d9a6df4e7a9: <div eID="gen11682" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen11681" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Complaints and Petitions.</title> <div sID="gen11683" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Save me, O God; for the waters are come in unto <hi type="italic">my</hi> soul. <hi type="super">2</hi> I sink in deep mire, where <hi type="italic">there is</hi> no standing: I am come into deep waters, where the floods overflow me. <hi type="super">3</hi> I am weary of my crying: my throat is dried: mine eyes fail while I wait for my God. <hi type="super">4</hi> They that hate me without a cause are more than the hairs of mine head: they that would destroy me, <hi type="italic">being</hi> mine enemies wrongfully, are mighty: then I restored <hi type="italic">that</hi> which I took not away. <hi type="super">5</hi> O God, thou knowest my foolishness; and my sins are not hid from thee. 6 Let not them that wait on thee, O Lord <hi type="small-caps">God</hi> of hosts, be ashamed for my sake: let not those that seek thee be confounded for my sake, O God of Israel. 7 Because for thy sake I have borne reproach; shame hath covered my face. <hi type="super">8</hi> I am become a stranger unto my brethren, and an alien unto my mother's children. <hi type="super">9</hi> For the zeal of thine house hath eaten me up; and the reproaches of them that reproached thee are fallen upon me. <hi type="super">10</hi> When I wept, <hi type="italic">and chastened</hi> my soul with fasting, that was to my reproach. <hi type="super">11</hi> I made sackcloth also my garment; and I became a proverb to them. <hi type="super">12</hi> They that sit in the gate speak against me; and I <hi type="italic">was</hi> the song of the drunkards. <div eID="gen11683" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11684" type="x-p"/> In these verses David complains of his troubles, intermixing with those complaints some requests for relief. <div eID="gen11684" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11685" type="x-p"/> I. His complaints are very sad, and he pours them out before the Lord, as one that hoped thus to ease himself of a burden that lay very heaven upon him. <div eID="gen11685" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11686" type="x-p"/> 1. He complains of the deep impressions that his troubles made upon his spirit (<reference osisRef="Ps.69.1-Ps.69.2">v. 1, 2</reference>): "The <hi type="italic">waters of affliction,</hi> those bitter waters, <hi type="italic">have come unto my soul,</hi> not only threaten my life, but disquiet my mind; they fill my head with perplexing cares and my heart with oppressive grief, so that I cannot enjoy God and myself as I used to do." We shall bear up under our troubles if we can but keep them from our hearts; but, when they put us out of the possession of our own souls, our case is bad. <hi type="italic">The spirit of a man will sustain his infirmity;</hi> but what shall we do when the spirit is wounded? That was David's case here. His thoughts sought for something to confide in, and with which to support his hope, but he found nothing: He sunk <hi type="italic">in deep mire, where there was no standing,</hi> no firm footing; the considerations that used to support and encourage him now failed him, or were out of the way, and he was ready to give himself up for gone. He sought for something to comfort himself with, but found himself <hi type="italic">in deep waters</hi> that <hi type="italic">overflowed</hi> him, overwhelmed him; he was like a sinking drowning man, in such confusion and consternation. This points at Christ's sufferings in his soul, and the inward agony he was in when he said, <hi type="italic">Now is my soul troubled;</hi> and, <hi type="italic">My soul is exceedingly sorrowful;</hi> for it was his soul that he made an offering for sin. And it instructs us, when we are in affliction, to commit the keeping of our souls to God, that we may be neither soured with discontent nor sink into despair. <div eID="gen11686" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11687" type="x-p"/> 2. He complains of the long continuance of his troubles (<reference osisRef="Ps.69.3">v. 3</reference>): <hi type="italic">I am weary of my crying.</hi> Though he could not keep his head above water, yet he cried to his God, and the more death was in his view the more life was in his prayers; yet he had not immediately an answer of peace given in, no, nor so much of that support and comfort in praying which God's people used to have; so that he was almost weary of crying, grew hoarse, and his <hi type="italic">throat</hi> so <hi type="italic">dried</hi> that he could cry no more. Nor had he his wonted satisfaction in believing, hoping, and expecting relief: <hi type="italic">My eyes fail while I wait for my God;</hi> he had almost looked his eyes out, in expectation of deliverance. Yet his pleading this with God is an indication that he is resolved not to give up believing and praying. His throat is dried, but his heart is not; his eyes fail, but his faith does not. Thus our Lord Jesus, on the cross, cried out, <hi type="italic">Why hast thou forsaken me?</hi> yet, at the same time, he kept hold of his relation to him: <hi type="italic">My God, my God.</hi> <div eID="gen11687" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11688" type="x-p"/> 3. He complains of the malice and multitude of his enemies, their injustice and cruelty, and the hardships they put upon him, <reference osisRef="Ps.69.4">v. 4</reference>. They hated him, they would destroy him, for hatred aims at the destruction of the person hated; but what was his iniquity, what was his sin, what provocation had he given them, that they were so spiteful towards him? None at all: "<hi type="italic">They hate me without a cause;</hi> I never did them the least injury, that they should bear me such ill-will." Our Saviour applies this to himself (<reference osisRef="John.15.25">John xv. 25</reference>): <hi type="italic">They hated me without a cause.</hi> We are apt to use this in justification of our passion against those that hate us, that we never gave them cause to hate us. But it is rather an argument why we should bear it patiently, because then we suffer as Christ did, and may then expect that God will give us redress. "They are <hi type="italic">my enemies wrongfully,</hi> for I have been no enemy to them." In a world where unrighteousness reigns so much we must not wonder if we meet with those that are our enemies wrongfully. Let us take care that we never do wrong and then we may the better bear it if we receive wrong. These enemies were not to be despised, but were very formidable both for their number—<hi type="italic">They are more than the hairs of my head</hi> (Christ's enemies were numerous; those that came to seize him were a great multitude; how were those increased that troubled him!) and for their strength—They <hi type="italic">are mighty</hi> in authority and power. We are weak, but our enemies are strong; for <hi type="italic">we wrestle against principalities and powers. Then I restored that which I took not away.</hi> Applying this to David, it was what his enemies compelled him to (they made him suffer for that offence which he had never been guilty of); and it was what he consented to, that, if possible, he might pacify them and make them to be at peace with him. He might have insisted upon the laws of justice and honour, the former not requiring and the latter commonly thought to forbid the restoring of that which we took not away, for that is to wrong ourselves both in our wealth and in our reputation. Yet the case may be such sometimes that it may become our duty. Blessed Paul, though free from all men, yet, for the honour of Christ and the edification of the church, made himself a servant to all. But, applying it to Christ, it is an observable description of the satisfaction which he made to God for our sin by his blood: <hi type="italic">Then he restored that which he took not away;</hi> he underwent the punishment that was due to us, paid our debt, suffered for our offence. God's glory, in some instances of it, was taken away by the sin of man; man's honour, and peace, and happiness, were taken away; it was not he that took them away, and yet by the merit of his death he restored them. <div eID="gen11688" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11689" type="x-p"/> 4. He complains of the unkindness of his friends and relations, and this is a grievance which with an ingenuous mind cuts as deeply as any (<reference osisRef="Ps.69.8">v. 8</reference>): "<hi type="italic">I have become a stranger to my brethren;</hi> they make themselves strange to me and use me as a stranger, are shy of conversing with me and ashamed to own me." This was fulfilled in Christ, whose <hi type="italic">brethren did not believe on him</hi> (<reference osisRef="John.7.5">John vii. 5</reference>), who <hi type="italic">came to his own and his own received him not</hi> (<reference osisRef="John.1.11">John i. 11</reference>), and who was forsaken by his disciples, whom he had been free with as his brethren. <div eID="gen11689" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11690" type="x-p"/> 5. He complains of the contempt that was put upon him and the reproach with which he was continually loaded. And in this especially his complaint points at Christ, who for our sakes submitted to the greatest disgrace and made himself of no reputation. We having by sin injured God in his honour, Christ made him satisfaction, not only by divesting himself of the honours due to an incarnate deity, but by submitting to the greatest dishonours that could be done to any man. Two things David here takes notice of as aggravations of the indignities done him:—(1.) The ground and matter of the reproach, <reference osisRef="Ps.69.10-Ps.69.11">v. 10, 11</reference>. They ridiculed him for that by which he both humbled himself and honoured God. When men lift up themselves in pride and vain glory they are justly laughed at for their folly; but David chastened his soul, and clothed himself with sackcloth, and from his abasing himself they took occasion to trample upon him. When men dishonour God it is just that their so doing should turn to their dishonour; but when David, purely in devotion to God and to testify his respect to him, <hi type="italic">wept, and chastened his soul with fasting,</hi> and <hi type="italic">made sackcloth his garment,</hi> as humble penitents used to do, instead of commending his devotion and recommending it as a great example of piety, they did all they could both to discourage him in it and to prevent others from following his good example; for <hi type="italic">that was to his reproach.</hi> They laughed at him as a fool for mortifying himself thus; and even for this he <hi type="italic">became a proverb to them;</hi> they made him the common subject of their banter. We must not think it strange if we be ill spoken of for that which is well done, and in which we have reason to hope that we are accepted of God. Our Lord Jesus was stoned for his good works (<reference osisRef="John.10.32">John x. 32</reference>), and when he cried, <hi type="italic">Eli, Eli—My God, my God,</hi> was bantered, as if he called for Elias. (2.) The persons that reproached him, <reference osisRef="Ps.69.12">v. 12</reference>. [1.] Even the gravest and the most honourable, from whom better was expected: <hi type="italic">Those that sit in the gate speak against me,</hi> and their reproaches pass for the dictates of senators and the decrees of judges, and are credited accordingly. [2.] The meanest, and the most despicable, the abjects (<reference osisRef="Ps.35.15">Ps. xxxv. 15</reference>), and scum of the country, the <hi type="italic">children of fools,</hi> yea, the <hi type="italic">children of base men,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.30.8">Job xxx. 8</reference>. Such drunkards as these make themselves vile, and he was the song of the drunkards; they made themselves and their companions merry with him. See the bad consequences of the sin of drunkenness; it makes men <hi type="italic">despisers of those that are good,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Tim.3.3">2 Tim. iii. 3</reference>. When <hi type="italic">the king was made sick with bottles of wine he stretched out his hand with scorners,</hi> <reference osisRef="Hos.7.5">Hos. vii. 5</reference>. The bench of the drunkards is the seat of the scornful. See what is commonly the lot of the best of men: those that are the praise of the wise are the song of fools. But it is easy to those that rightly judge of things to despise being thus despised. <div eID="gen11690" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11691" type="x-p"/> II. His confessions of sin are very serious (<reference osisRef="Ps.69.5">v. 5</reference>): "<hi type="italic">O God! thou knowest my foolishness,</hi> what is and what is not; my sins that I am guilty of are not hidden from thee, and therefore thou knowest how innocent I am of those crimes which they charge upon me." Note, Even when, as to men's unjust accusations, we plead <hi type="italic">Not guilty,</hi> yet, before God, we must acknowledge ourselves to have deserved all that is brought upon us, and much worse. This is the genuine confession of a penitent, who knows that he cannot prosper in covering his sin, and that <hi type="italic">therefore</hi> it is his wisdom to acknowledge it, because it is naked and open before God. 1. He knows the corruption of our nature: <hi type="italic">Thou knowest the foolishness</hi> that is bound up in my heart. All our sins take rise from our foolishness. 2. He knows the transgressions of our lives; they are not hidden from him, no, not our heart-sins, no, not those that are committed most secretly. They are all done in his sight, and are never cast behind his back till they are repented of and pardoned. This may aptly be applied to Christ, for he knew no sin, yet he was made sin for us; and God knew it, nor was it hidden from him, when it pleased the Lord to bruise him and put him to grief. <div eID="gen11691" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11692" type="x-p"/> III. His supplications are very earnest. 1. For himself (<reference osisRef="Ps.69.1">v. 1</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Save me, O God!</hi> save me from sinking, from despairing." Thus Christ was heard in that he feared, for he was saved from letting fall his undertaking, <reference osisRef="Heb.5.7">Heb. v. 7</reference>. 2. For his friends (<reference osisRef="Ps.69.6">v. 6</reference>): <hi type="italic">Let not those that wait on thee, O Lord God of hosts! and that seek thee, O God of Israel!</hi> (under these two characters we ought to seek God, and in seeking him to wait on him, as the <hi type="italic">God of hosts,</hi> who has all power to help, and as the <hi type="italic">God of Israel</hi> in covenant with his people, whom therefore he is engaged in honour and truth to help) <hi type="italic">be ashamed and confounded for my sake.</hi> This intimates his fear that if God did not appear for him it would be a discouragement to all other good people and would give their enemies occasion to triumph over them, and his earnest desire that whatever became of him all that seek God, and wait upon him, might be kept in heart and kept in countenance, and might neither be discouraged in themselves nor exposed to contempt from others. If Jesus Christ had not been owned and accepted of his Father in his sufferings, all that seek God, and wait for him, would have been ashamed and confounded; but they have confidence towards God, and in his name come boldly to the throne of grace. <div eID="gen11692" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11693" type="x-p"/> IV. His plea is very powerful, <reference osisRef="Ps.69.7">v. 7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.69.9">9</reference>. Reproach was one of the greatest of his burdens: "Lord, roll away the reproach, and plead my cause, for, 1. It is for thee that I am reproached, for serving thee and trusting in thee: <hi type="italic">For thy sake I have borne reproach.</hi>" Those that are evil spoken of for well-doing may with a humble confidence leave it to God to <hi type="italic">bring forth their righteousness as the light.</hi> 2. "It is with thee that I am reproached: <hi type="italic">The zeal of thy house has eaten me up,</hi> that is, has made me forget myself, and do that which they wickedly turn to my reproach. Those that hate thee and thy house for that reason hate me, because they know how zealously affected I am to it. It is this that has made them ready to eat me up and has eaten up all the love and respect I had among them." Those that blasphemed God, and spoke ill of his word and ways, did therefore reproach David for believing in his word and walking in his ways. Or it may be construed as an instance of David's zeal for God's house, that he resented all the indignities done to God's name as if they had been done to his own name. He laid to heart all the dishonour done to God and the contempt cast upon religion; these he laid nearer to his heart than any outward troubles of his own. And <hi type="italic">therefore</hi> he had reason to hope God would interest himself in the reproaches cast upon him, because he had always interested himself in the reproaches cast upon God. Both the parts of <reference osisRef="Ps.69.9">this verse</reference> are applied to Christ. (1.) It was an instance of his love to his Father that <hi type="italic">the zeal of his house did even eat him up</hi> when he whipped the buyers and sellers out of the temple, which reminded his disciples of this text, <reference osisRef="John.2.17">John ii. 17</reference>. (2.) It was an instance of his self-denial, and that he pleased not himself, that the <hi type="italic">reproaches of those that reproached God fell upon him</hi> (<reference osisRef="Rom.15.3">Rom. xv. 3</reference>), and therein he set us an example.
entries.194bb5341ec7752d76e5034cc06c6d9be6c3031f: <div eID="gen11693" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Complaints and Petitions.</title> <div sID="gen11694" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">13</hi> But as for me, my prayer <hi type="italic">is</hi> unto thee, <hi type="small-caps">O Lord</hi> , <hi type="italic">in</hi> an acceptable time: O God, in the multitude of thy mercy hear me, in the truth of thy salvation. <hi type="super">14</hi> Deliver me out of the mire, and let me not sink: let me be delivered from them that hate me, and out of the deep waters. <hi type="super">15</hi> Let not the waterflood overflow me, neither let the deep swallow me up, and let not the pit shut her mouth upon me. <hi type="super">16</hi> Hear me, <hi type="small-caps">O Lord</hi> ; for thy lovingkindness <hi type="italic">is</hi> good: turn unto me according to the multitude of thy tender mercies. <hi type="super">17</hi> And hide not thy face from thy servant; for I am in trouble: hear me speedily. <hi type="super">18</hi> Draw nigh unto my soul, <hi type="italic">and</hi> redeem it: deliver me because of mine enemies. <hi type="super">19</hi> Thou hast known my reproach, and my shame, and my dishonour: mine adversaries <hi type="italic">are</hi> all before thee. 20 Reproach hath broken my heart; and I am full of heaviness: and I looked <hi type="italic">for some</hi> to take pity, but <hi type="italic">there was</hi> none; and for comforters, but I found none. <hi type="super">21</hi> They gave me also gall for my meat; and in my thirst they gave me vinegar to drink. <div eID="gen11694" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11695" type="x-p"/> David had been speaking before of the spiteful reproaches which his enemies cast upon him; here he adds, <hi type="italic">But, as for me, my prayer is unto thee.</hi> They spoke ill of him for his fasting and praying, and for that he was made the song of the drunkards; but, notwithstanding that, he resolves to continue praying. Note, Though we may be jeered for well-doing, we must never be jeered out of it. Those can bear but little for God, and their confessing his name before men, that cannot bear a scoff and a hard word rather than quit their duty. David's enemies were very abusive to him, but this was his comfort, that he had a God to go to, with whom he would lodge his cause. "They think to carry their cause by insolence and calumny; but I use other methods. Whatever they do, <hi type="italic">As for me, my prayer is unto thee, O Lord!</hi>" And it was in an acceptable time, not the less acceptable for being a time of affliction. God will not drive us from him, though it is need that drives us to him; nay, it is the more acceptable, because the misery and distress of God's people make them so much the more the objects of his pity: it is seasonable for him to help them when all other helps fail, and they are undone, and feel that they are undone, if he do not help them. We find this expression used concerning Christ. <reference osisRef="Isa.49.8">Isa. xlix. 8</reference>, <hi type="italic">In an acceptable time have I heard thee.</hi> Now observe, <div eID="gen11695" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11696" type="x-p"/> I. What his requests are. 1. That he might have a gracious audience given to his complaints, the cry of his affliction, and the desire of his heart. <hi type="italic">Hear me</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.69.13">v. 13</reference>), and again, <hi type="italic">Hear me, O Lord!</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.69.16">v. 16</reference>), <hi type="italic">Hear me speedily</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.69.17">v. 17</reference>), not only hear what I say, but grant what I ask. Christ knew that <hi type="italic">the Father heard him always,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.11.42">John xi. 42</reference>. 2. That he might be rescued out of his troubles, might be saved from sinking under the load of grief (<hi type="italic">Deliver me out of the mire;</hi> let me not stick in it, so some, but help me out, and <hi type="italic">set my feet on a rock,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.40.2">Ps. xl. 2</reference>), might be saved from his enemies, that they might not swallow him up, nor have their will against him: "<hi type="italic">Let me be delivered from those that hate me,</hi> as a lamb from the paw of a lion, <reference osisRef="Ps.69.14">v. 14</reference>. Though I have come into deep waters (<reference osisRef="Ps.69.2">v. 2</reference>), where I am ready to conclude that the floods will overflow me, yet let my fears be prevented and silenced; let not the waterflood, though it flow upon me, overflow me, <reference osisRef="Ps.69.15">v. 15</reference>. Let me not fall into the gulf of despair; let not that deep swallow me up; let not that pit shut her mouth upon me, for then I am undone." He gave himself up for lost in the beginning of the psalm; yet now he has his head above water, and is not so weary of crying as he thought himself. 3. That God would turn to him (<reference osisRef="Ps.69.16">v. 16</reference>), that he would smile upon him, and not hide his face from him, <reference osisRef="Ps.69.17">v. 17</reference>. The tokens of God's favour to us, and the light of his countenance shining upon us, are enough to keep our spirits from sinking in the deepest mire of outward troubles, nor need we desire any more to make us safe and easy, <reference osisRef="Ps.69.18">v. 18</reference>. "Draw nigh to my soul, to manifest thyself to it, and that shall redeem it." <div eID="gen11696" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11697" type="x-p"/> II. What his pleas are to enforce these petitions. 1. He pleads God's mercy and truth (<reference osisRef="Ps.69.13">v. 13</reference>): <hi type="italic">In the multitude of thy mercy hear me.</hi> There is mercy in God, a multitude of mercies, all kinds of mercy, inexhaustible mercy, mercy enough for all, enough for each; and hence we must take our encouragement in praying. The truth also of his salvation (the truth of all those promises of salvation which he has made to those that trust in him) is a further encouragement. He repeats his argument taken from the mercy of God: "<hi type="italic">Hear me,</hi> for <hi type="italic">thy lovingkindness is good.</hi> It is so in itself; it is rich and plentiful and abundant. It is so in the account of all the saints; it is very precious to them, it is their life, their joy, their all. O let me have the benefit of it! Turn to me, <hi type="italic">according to the multitude of thy tender mercies,</hi>" <reference osisRef="Ps.69.16">v. 16</reference>. See how highly he speaks of the goodness of God: in him there are mercies, tender mercies, and a multitude of them. If we think well of God, and continue to do so under the greatest hardships, we need not fear but God will do well for us; for <hi type="italic">he takes pleasure in those that hope in his mercy,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.147.11">Ps. cxlvii. 11</reference>. 2. He pleads his own distress and affliction: "<hi type="italic">Hide not thy face</hi> from me, <hi type="italic">for I am in trouble</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.69.17">v. 17</reference>), and therefore need thy favour; therefore it will come seasonably, and therefore I shall know how to value it." He pleads particularly the reproach he was under and the indignities that were done him (<reference osisRef="Ps.69.19">v. 19</reference>): <hi type="italic">Thou hast known my reproach, my shame, and my dishonour.</hi> See what a stress is laid upon this; for, in the sufferings of Christ for us, perhaps nothing contributed more to the satisfaction he made for sin, which had been so injurious to God in his honour, than the reproach, and shame, and dishonour he underwent, which God took notice of, and accepted as more than an equivalent for the everlasting shame and contempt which our sins had deserved, and therefore we must by repentance take shame to ourselves and bear the reproach of our youth. And if at any time we be called out to suffer reproach, and shame, and dishonour, for his sake, this may be our comfort, that he knows it, and, as he is before-hand with us, so he will not be behind-hand with us. The Psalmist speaks the language of an ingenuous nature when he says (<reference osisRef="Ps.69.20">v. 20</reference>): <hi type="italic">Reproach has broken my heart; I am full of heaviness;</hi> for it bears hard upon one that knows the worth of a good name to be put under a bad character; but when we consider what an honour it is to be dishonoured for God, and what a favour to be counted worthy to suffer shame for his name (as they deemed it, <reference osisRef="Acts.5.41">Acts v. 41</reference>), we shall see there is no reason at all why it should sit so heavily or be any heart-breaking to us. 3. He pleads the insolence and cruelty of his enemies (<reference osisRef="Ps.69.18">v. 18</reference>): <hi type="italic">Deliver me because of my enemies,</hi> because they were such as he had before described them, <reference osisRef="Ps.69.4">v. 4</reference>. "<hi type="italic">My adversaries are all before thee</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.69.19">v. 19</reference>); thou knowest what sort of men they are, what danger I am in from them, what enemies they are to thee, and how much thou art reflected upon in what they do and design against me." One instance of their barbarity is given (<reference osisRef="Ps.69.21">v. 21</reference>): <hi type="italic">They gave me gall for my meat</hi> (the word signifies a bitter herb, and is often joined with wormwood) <hi type="italic">and in my thirst they gave me vinegar to drink.</hi> This was literally fulfilled in Christ, and did so directly point to him that he would not say <hi type="italic">It is finished</hi> till this was fulfilled; and, in order that his enemies might have occasion to fulfil it, he said, <hi type="italic">I thirst,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.19.28-John.19.29">John xix. 28, 29</reference>. Some think that the hyssop which they put to his mouth with the vinegar was the bitter herb which they gave him with the vinegar for his meat. See how particularly the sufferings of Christ were foretold, which proves the scripture to be the word of God, and how exactly the predictions were fulfilled in Jesus Christ, which proves him to be the true Messiah. This is he that should come, and we are to look for no other. 4. He pleads the unkindness of his friends and his disappointment in them (<reference osisRef="Ps.69.20">v. 20</reference>): <hi type="italic">I looked for some to take pity, but there was none;</hi> they all failed him like the brooks in summer. This was fulfilled in Christ, for in his sufferings all his disciples forsook him and fled. We cannot expect too little from men (miserable comforters are they all); nor can we expect too much from God, for he is the Father of mercy and the God of all comfort and consolation.
entries.b56a424f5daec5d9675aedb007683d814baddfb9: <div eID="gen11697" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Pleading with God; Prophetic Imprecations.</title> <div sID="gen11698" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">22</hi> Let their table become a snare before them: and <hi type="italic">that which should have been</hi> for <hi type="italic">their</hi> welfare, <hi type="italic">let it become</hi> a trap. <hi type="super">23</hi> Let their eyes be darkened, that they see not; and make their loins continually to shake. 24 Pour out thine indignation upon them, and let thy wrathful anger take hold of them. <hi type="super">25</hi> Let their habitation be desolate; <hi type="italic">and</hi> let none dwell in their tents. <hi type="super">26</hi> For they persecute <hi type="italic">him</hi> whom thou hast smitten; and they talk to the grief of those whom thou hast wounded. <hi type="super">27</hi> Add iniquity unto their iniquity: and let them not come into thy righteousness. 28 Let them be blotted out of the book of the living, and not be written with the righteous. <hi type="super">29</hi> But I <hi type="italic">am</hi> poor and sorrowful: let thy salvation, O God, set me up on high. <div eID="gen11698" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11699" type="x-p"/> These imprecations are not David's prayers against his enemies, but prophecies of the destruction of Christ's persecutors, especially the Jewish nation, which our Lord himself foretold with tears, and which was accomplished about forty years after the death of Christ. The first two verses of this paragraph are expressly applied to the judgments of God upon the unbelieving Jews by the apostle (<reference osisRef="Ps.69.22-Ps.69.23">Rom. xi. 9</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rom.11.9-Rom.11.10">10</reference>), and therefore the whole must look that way. The rejection of the Jews for rejecting Christ, as it was a signal instance of God's justice and an earnest of the vengeance which God will at last take on all that are obstinate in their infidelity, so it was, and continues to be, a convincing proof of the truth of the Christian religion. One great objection against it, at first, was, that it set aside the ceremonial law; but its doing so was effectually justified, and that objection removed, when God so remarkably set it aside by the utter destruction of the temple, and the sinking of those, with the Mosaic economy, that obstinately adhered to it in opposition to the gospel of Christ. Let us observe here, <div eID="gen11699" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11700" type="x-p"/> I. What the judgments are which should come upon the crucifiers of Christ; not upon all of them, for there were those who had a hand in his death and yet repented and found mercy (<reference osisRef="Acts.2.23">Acts ii. 23</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.3.14-Acts.3.15">iii. 14, 15</reference>), but upon those of them and their successors who justified it by an obstinate infidelity and rejection of his gospel, and by an inveterate enmity to his disciples and followers. See <reference osisRef="1Thess.2.15-1Thess.2.16">1 Thess. ii. 15, 16</reference>. It is here foretold, <div eID="gen11700" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11701" type="x-p"/> 1. That their sacrifices and offerings should be a mischief and prejudice to them (<reference osisRef="Ps.69.22">v. 22</reference>): <hi type="italic">Let their table become a snare.</hi> This may be understood of the altar of the Lord, which is called <hi type="italic">his table and theirs</hi> because in feasting upon the sacrifices they were partakers of the altar. This should have been for their welfare or peace (for they were peace-offerings), but it became a snare and a trap to them; for by their affection and adherence to the altar they were held fast in their infidelity and hardened in their prejudices against Christ, that altar which those had no right to eat of who continued to serve the tabernacle, <reference osisRef="Heb.13.10">Heb. xiii. 10</reference>. Or it may be understood of their common creature-comforts, even their necessary food; they had given Christ gall and vinegar, and therefore justly shall their meat and drink be made gall and vinegar to them. When the supports of life and delights of sense, through the corruption of our nature, become an occasion of sin to us, and are made the food and fuel of our sensuality, then our table is a snare, which is a good reason why we should never feed ourselves without fear, <reference osisRef="Jude.1.12">Jude 12</reference>. <div eID="gen11701" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11702" type="x-p"/> 2. That they should never have the comfort either of that knowledge or of that peace which believers are blessed with in the gospel of Christ (<reference osisRef="Ps.69.23">v. 23</reference>), that they should be given up, (1.) To a judicial blindness: <hi type="italic">Let their eyes be darkened,</hi> that they see not the glory of God in the face of Christ. Their sin was that they would not see, but shut their eyes against the light, loving darkness rather; their punishment was that they should not see, but be given up to their own hearts' lusts, which were hardening, and the god of this world should be permitted to blind their minds, <reference osisRef="2Cor.4.4">2 Cor. iv. 4</reference>. This was foretold concerning them (<reference osisRef="Isa.6.10">Isa. vi. 10</reference>), and Christ ratified it, <reference osisRef="Matt.13.14-Matt.13.15">Matt. xiii. 14, 15</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.12.40">John xii. 40</reference>. (2.) To a judicial terror. There is a gracious terror, which opens the way to comfort, such as that of Paul (<reference osisRef="Acts.9.6">Acts ix. 6</reference>); he trembled and was astonished. But this is a terror that shall never end in peace, but shall make their loins continually to shake, through horror of conscience, as Belshazzar, when the joints of his loins were loosed. "Let them be driven to despair, and filled with constant confusion." This was fulfilled in the desperate counsels of the Jews when the Romans came upon them. <div eID="gen11702" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11703" type="x-p"/> 3. That they should fall and lie under God's anger and fiery indignation (<reference osisRef="Ps.69.24">v. 24</reference>): <hi type="italic">Pour out thy indignation upon them.</hi> Note, Those who reject God's great salvation proffered to them may justly fear that his indignation will be poured out upon them; for those that submit not to the Son of his love will certainly be made the generation of his wrath. It is the doom passed on those who believe not in Christ that the <hi type="italic">wrath of God abideth on them</hi> (<reference osisRef="John.3.36">John iii. 36</reference>); it takes hold of them, and will never let them go. Salvation itself will not save those that are not willing to be ruled by it. Behold the goodness and severity of God! <div eID="gen11703" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11704" type="x-p"/> 4. That their place and nation should be utterly taken away, the very thing they were afraid of, and to prevent which, as they pretended, they persecuted Christ (<reference osisRef="John.11.48">John xi. 48</reference>): <hi type="italic">Let their habitation be desolate</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.69.25">v. 25</reference>), which was fulfilled when their country was laid waste by the Romans, and <hi type="italic">Zion, for their sakes, was ploughed as a field,</hi> <reference osisRef="Mic.3.12">Mic. iii. 12</reference>. The temple was the house which they were in a particular manner proud of, but this was <hi type="italic">left unto them desolate,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.23.38">Matt. xxiii. 38</reference>. Yet that is not all; it ought to be some satisfaction to us, if we be cut off from the enjoyment of our possessions, that others will have the benefit of them when we are dislodged: but it is here added, <hi type="italic">Let none dwell in their tents,</hi> which was remarkably fulfilled in Judah and Jerusalem, for after the destruction of the Jews it was long ere the country was inhabited to any purpose. But this is applied particularly to Judas, by St. Peter, <reference osisRef="Acts.1.20">Acts i. 20</reference>. For, he being <hi type="italic">felo de se—a suicide,</hi> we may suppose his estate was confiscated, so that <hi type="italic">his habitation was desolate and no man</hi> of his own kindred <hi type="italic">dwelt therein.</hi> <div eID="gen11704" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11705" type="x-p"/> 5. That their way to ruin should be downhill, and nothing should stop them, nor interpose to prevent it (<reference osisRef="Ps.69.27">v. 27</reference>): "Lord, leave them to themselves, to <hi type="italic">add iniquity to iniquity.</hi>" Those that are bad, if they be given up to their own hearts' lusts, will certainly be worse; they will add sin to sin, nay, they will <hi type="italic">add rebellion to their sin,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.34.37">Job xxxiv. 37</reference>. It is said of the Jews that they <hi type="italic">filled up their sin always,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Thess.2.16">1 Thess. ii. 16</reference>. <hi type="italic">Add the punishment of iniquity to their iniquity</hi> (so some read it), for the same word signifies both sin and punishment, so close is their connexion. If men will sin, God will reckon for it. But those that have multiplied to sin may yet find mercy, for God multiplies to pardon, through the righteousness of the Mediator; and therefore, that they might be precluded from all hopes of mercy, he adds, <hi type="italic">Let them not come into thy righteousness,</hi> to receive the benefit of the righteousness of God, which is by faith in a Mediator, <reference osisRef="Phil.3.9">Phil. iii. 9</reference>. Not that God shuts out any from that righteousness, for the gospel excludes none that do not by their unbelief exclude themselves; but let them be left to take their own course and they will never come into this government; for being ignorant of the demands of God's righteousness, and going about to establish the merit of their own, they <hi type="italic">have not submitted themselves to the righteousness of God,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rom.10.3">Rom. x. 3</reference>. And those that are so proud and self-willed that they will not come into God's righteousness shall have their doom accordingly; they themselves have decided it: they <hi type="italic">shall not come into his righteousness.</hi> Let not those expect any benefit by it that are not willing and glad to be beholden to it. <div eID="gen11705" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11706" type="x-p"/> 6. That they should be cut off from all hopes of happiness (<reference osisRef="Ps.69.28">v. 28</reference>): <hi type="italic">Let them be blotted out of the book of the living;</hi> let them not be suffered to live any longer, since, the longer they live, the more mischief they do. Multitudes of the unbelieving Jews fell by sword and famine, and none of those who had embraced the Christian faith perished among them; the nation, as a nation, was blotted out, and became not a people. Many understand it of their rejection from God's covenant and all the privileges of it; that is <hi type="italic">the book of the living:</hi> "Let the commonwealth of Israel itself, Israel according to the flesh, now become alienated from that covenant of promise which hitherto it has had the monopoly of. Let it appear that they were never written in the Lamb's book of life, but reprobate silver let <hi type="italic">men call them, because the Lord has rejected them.</hi> Let them <hi type="italic">not be written with the righteous;</hi> that is, let them not have a place in the congregation of the saints when they shall all be gathered in the general assembly of those whose names are written in heaven," <reference osisRef="Ps.1.5">Ps. i. 5</reference>. <div eID="gen11706" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11707" type="x-p"/> II. What the sin is for which these dreadful judgments should be brought upon them (<reference osisRef="Ps.69.26">v. 26</reference>): <hi type="italic">They persecute him whom thou hast smitten, and talk to the grief of thy wounded.</hi> 1. Christ was he whom God had smitten, for <hi type="italic">it pleased the Lord to bruise him,</hi> and he was esteemed <hi type="italic">stricken, smitten of God, and afflicted,</hi> and therefore men <hi type="italic">hid their faces from him,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.53.3-Isa.53.4">Isa. liii. 3, 4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.53.10">10</reference>. They persecuted him with a rage reaching up to heaven; they cried, <hi type="italic">Crucify him, crucify him.</hi> Compare that of St. Peter with this, <reference osisRef="Acts.2.23">Acts ii. 23</reference>. Though he was <hi type="italic">delivered by the counsel and foreknowledge of God,</hi> it was <hi type="italic">with wicked hands that they crucified and slew him.</hi> They talked to the grief of the Lord Jesus when he was upon the cross, saying, <hi type="italic">He trusted in God, let him deliver him,</hi> than which nothing could be said more grieving. 2. The suffering saints were God's wounded, wounded in his cause and for his sake, and them they persecuted, and <hi type="italic">talked to their grief.</hi> For these things <hi type="italic">wrath came upon them to the uttermost,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Thess.2.16">1 Thess. ii. 16</reference>; and see <reference osisRef="Matt.23.34-Matt.23.36">Matt. xxiii. 34</reference>, &c. This may be understood more generally, and it teaches us that nothing is more provoking to God than to insult over those whom he has smitten, and to add affliction to the afflicted, upon which it justly follows here, <hi type="italic">Add iniquity to iniquity;</hi> see <reference osisRef="Zech.1.15">Zech. i. 15</reference>. Those that are of a wounded spirit, under trouble and fear about their spiritual state, ought to be very tenderly dealt with, and care must be taken not to <hi type="italic">talk to their grief and not to make the heart of the righteous sad.</hi> <div eID="gen11707" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11708" type="x-p"/> III. What the psalmist thinks of himself in the midst of all (<reference osisRef="Ps.69.29">v. 29</reference>): "<hi type="italic">But I am poor and sorrowful;</hi> that is the worst of my case, under outward afflictions, yet <hi type="italic">written among the righteous,</hi> and not under God's indignation as they are." It is better to be poor and sorrowful, with the blessing of God, than rich and jovial and under his curse. For those who come into God's righteousness shall soon see an end of their poverty and sorrow, and his salvation shall set them up on high, which is the thing that David here prays for, <reference osisRef="Isa.61.10">Isa. lxi. 10</reference>. This may be applied to Christ. He was, in his humiliation, poor and sorrowful, a man of sorrows, and that had not where to lay his head. But God highly exalted him; the salvation wrought for him, the salvation wrought by him, <hi type="italic">set him up on high, far above all principalities and powers.</hi>
entries.bc640f62e8e43f35d5581604488e789c2627eba9: <div eID="gen11708" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Comfort for the Persecuted; Thanksgiving and Praise.</title> <div sID="gen11709" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">30</hi> I will praise the name of God with a song, and will magnify him with thanksgiving. <hi type="super">31</hi> <hi type="italic">This</hi> also shall please the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> better than an ox <hi type="italic">or</hi> bullock that hath horns and hoofs. <hi type="super">32</hi> The humble shall see <hi type="italic">this, and</hi> be glad: and your heart shall live that seek God. <hi type="super">33</hi> For the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> heareth the poor, and despiseth not his prisoners. <hi type="super">34</hi> Let the heaven and earth praise him, the seas, and every thing that moveth therein. <hi type="super">35</hi> For God will save Zion, and will build the cities of Judah: that they may dwell there, and have it in possession. <hi type="super">36</hi> The seed also of his servants shall inherit it: and they that love his name shall dwell therein. <div eID="gen11709" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11710" type="x-p"/> The psalmist here, both as a type of Christ and as an example to Christians, concludes a psalm with holy joy and praise which he began with complaints and remonstrances of his griefs. <div eID="gen11710" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11711" type="x-p"/> I. He resolves to praise God himself, not doubting but that therein he should be accepted of him (<reference osisRef="Ps.69.30-Ps.69.31">v. 30, 31</reference>): "<hi type="italic">I will praise the name of God,</hi> not only with my heart, but with my song, and <hi type="italic">magnify him with thanksgiving;</hi>" for he is pleased to reckon himself magnified by the thankful praises of his people. It is intimated that all Christians ought to glorify God with their praises, <hi type="italic">in psalms, and hymns, and spiritual songs.</hi> And <hi type="italic">this shall please the Lord,</hi> through Christ the Mediator of our praises as well as of our prayers, better than the most valuable of the legal sacrifices (<reference osisRef="Ps.69.31">v. 31</reference>), <hi type="italic">an ox or bullock.</hi> This is a plain intimation that in the days of the Messiah an end should be put, not only to the sacrifices of atonement, but to those of praise and acknowledgment which were instituted by the ceremonial law; and, instead of them, spiritual sacrifices of praise and thanksgiving are accepted—the calves of our lips, not the calves of the stall, <reference osisRef="Heb.13.15">Heb. xiii. 15</reference>. It is a great comfort to us that humble and thankful praises are more pleasing to God than the most costly pompous sacrifices are or ever were. <div eID="gen11711" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11712" type="x-p"/> II. He encourages other good people to rejoice in God and continue seeking him (<reference osisRef="Ps.69.32-Ps.69.33">v. 32, 33</reference>): <hi type="italic">The humble shall see this and be glad.</hi> They shall observe, to their comfort, 1. The experiences of the saints. They shall see how ready God is to hear the poor when they cry to him, and to give them that which they call upon him for, how far he is from despising his prisoners; though men despise them, he favours them with his gracious visits and will find a time to enlarge them. <hi type="italic">The humble shall see this and be glad,</hi> not only because when one member is honoured all the members rejoice with it, but because it is an encouragement to them in their straits and difficulties to trust in God. It shall revive the hearts of those who seek God to see more seals and subscriptions to this truth, that Jacob's God never said to Jacob's seed, <hi type="italic">Seek you me in vain.</hi> 2. The exaltation of the Saviour, for of him the psalmist had been speaking, and of himself as a type of him. When his sorrows are over, and he enters into the joy that was set before him, when he is heard and discharged from his imprisonment in the grave, the humble shall look upon it and be glad, and those that seek God through Christ shall live and be comforted, concluding that, if they suffer with him, they shall also reign with him. <div eID="gen11712" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11713" type="x-p"/> III. He calls upon all the creatures to praise God, the heaven, and earth, and sea, and the inhabitants of each, <reference osisRef="Ps.69.34">v. 34</reference>. Heaven and earth, and the hosts of both, were made by him, and therefore <hi type="italic">let heaven and earth praise him.</hi> Angels in heaven, and saints on earth, may each of them in their respective habitations furnish themselves with matter enough for constant praise. Let the fishes of the sea, though mute to a proverb, praise the Lord, for the sea is his, and he made it. The praises of the world must be offered for God's favours to his church, <reference osisRef="Ps.69.35-Ps.69.36">v. 35, 36</reference>. For God will save Zion, the holy mountain, where his service was kept up. He will save all that are sanctified and set apart to him, all that employ themselves in his worship, and all those over whom Christ reigns; for he was King upon the holy hill of Zion. He has mercy in store for the cities of Judah, of which tribe Christ was. God will do great things for the gospel church, in which let all that wish well to it rejoice. For, 1. It shall be peopled and inhabited. There shall be added to it such as shall be saved. <hi type="italic">The cities of Judah shall be built,</hi> particular churches shall be formed and incorporated according to the gospel model, that there may be a remnant to <hi type="italic">dwell there</hi> and to <hi type="italic">have it in possession,</hi> to enjoy the privileges conferred upon it and to pay the tributes and services required from it. Those that love his name, that have a kindness for religion in general, shall embrace the Christian religion, and take their place in the Christian church; they shall dwell therein, as citizens, and of the household of God 2. It shall be perpetuated and inherited. Christianity was not to be <hi type="italic">res unius ætatis—a transitory thin.</hi> No: <hi type="italic">The seed of his servants shall inherit it.</hi> God will secure and raise up for himself a seed to serve him, and they shall inherit the privileges of their fathers; for the promise is to you and your children, as it was of old. <hi type="italic">I will be a God to thee, and thy seed after thee.</hi> The land of promise shall never be lost for want of heirs, for God <hi type="italic">can out of stones raise up children unto Abraham</hi> and will do so rather than the entail shall be cut off. David shall never want a man to stand before him. The Redeemer shall see his seed, and prolong his days in them, till the mystery of God shall be finished and the mystical body completed. And since the holy seed is the substance of the world, and if that were all gathered in the world would be at an end quickly, it is just that for this assurance of the preservation of it heaven and earth should praise him.  <chapter eID="Ps.69"/> <div eID="gen11713" type="x-p"/>

entries.d7cf63c873f53388172a7c29d4048553fc6ee163: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6252"/><title type="x-s2">PSALM 69</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Ps.69.1-Ps.69.36">Psa 69:1-36</reference>. Upon Shoshannim--(See on <reference osisRef="Ps.45.1">Psa 45:1</reference>, title). Mingling the language of prayer and complaint, the sufferer, whose condition is here set forth, pleads for God's help as one suffering in His cause, implores the divine retribution on his malicious enemies, and, viewing his deliverance as sure, promises praise by himself, and others, to whom God will extend like blessings. This Psalm is referred to seven times in the New Testament as prophetical of Christ and the gospel times. Although the character in which the Psalmist appears to some in <reference osisRef="Ps.69.5">Psa 69:5</reference> is that of a sinner, yet his condition as a sufferer innocent of alleged crimes sustains the typical character of the composition, and it may be therefore regarded throughout, as the twenty-second, as typically expressive of the feelings of our Saviour in the flesh.</title> <div sID="gen9569" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6252"/>1-2. (Compare <reference osisRef="Ps.40.2">Psa 40:2</reference>).<div eID="gen9569" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9570" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">come in unto my soul--</hi>literally, "come even to my soul," endanger my life by drowning (<reference osisRef="Jonah.2.5">Jon 2:5</reference>). <div eID="gen9570" type="x-p"/>
entries.98df2df465ccfd04e80d23ab3cea06a48fecd32f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6253"/><div sID="gen9571" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6253"/>3. (Compare <reference osisRef="Ps.6.6">Psa 6:6</reference>).<div eID="gen9571" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9572" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">mine eyes fail--</hi>in watching (<reference osisRef="Ps.119.82">Psa 119:82</reference>). <div eID="gen9572" type="x-p"/>
entries.544e76acef8d485df3d0524cf44c1f222d95323a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6254"/><div sID="gen9573" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6254"/><hi type="bold">4. hate me, &c.--</hi>(Compare <reference osisRef="John.15.25">Joh 15:25</reference>). On the number and power of his enemies (compare <reference osisRef="Ps.40.12">Psa 40:12</reference>).<div eID="gen9573" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9574" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">then I restored ... away--</hi>that is, he suffered wrongfully under the imputation of robbery. <div eID="gen9574" type="x-p"/>
entries.5dc6da42812684f767568ee501b1058a44589282: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6255"/><div sID="gen9575" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6255"/>5. This may be regarded as an appeal, vindicating his innocence, as if he had said, "If sinful, thou knowest," &c. Though David's condition as a sufferer may typify Christ's, without requiring that a parallel be found in character. <div eID="gen9575" type="x-p"/>
entries.a9ce4bdb6df3a9402e0ef12355ed00bcae6e8876: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6256"/><div sID="gen9576" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6256"/><hi type="bold">6. for my sake--</hi>literally, "in me," in my confusion and shame. <div eID="gen9576" type="x-p"/>
entries.5ee411a2fc1c40ea6c8539ff754348ca6301819e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6257"/><div sID="gen9577" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6257"/>7-12. This plea contemplates his relation to God as a sufferer in His cause. Reproach, domestic estrangement (<reference osisRef="Mark.3.21">Mr 3:21</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.7.5">Joh 7:5</reference>), exhaustion in God's service (<reference osisRef="John.2.17">Joh 2:17</reference>), revilings and taunts of base men were the sufferings. <div eID="gen9577" type="x-p"/>
entries.5fed7d11640608cfe5bc2e32a04ad16028b70e56: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6260"/><div sID="gen9580" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6260"/>13-15. With increasing reliance on God, he prays for help, describing his distress in the figures of <reference osisRef="Ps.69.1">Psa 69:1</reference>, 2. <div eID="gen9580" type="x-p"/>
entries.069d628b1e0e93dca8d8ae9558a8665587c5a542: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6261"/><div sID="gen9581" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6261"/>16-18. These earnest terms are often used, and the address to God, as indifferent or averse, is found in <reference osisRef="Ps.3.7">Psa 3:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.22.24">22:24</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.27.9">27:9</reference>, &c. <div eID="gen9581" type="x-p"/>
entries.17e1b4c761e388dbd2e7c16a0de688dee87bd252: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6262"/><div sID="gen9582" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6262"/>19-20. Calling God to witness his distress, he presents its aggravation produced by the want of sympathizing friends (compare <reference osisRef="Isa.63.5">Is 63:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Mark.14.50">Mr 14:50</reference>). <div eID="gen9582" type="x-p"/>
entries.2c0de9201364e6a397dac45595bbab937ce7bda1: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6263"/><div sID="gen9583" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6263"/>21. Instead of such, his enemies increase his pain by giving him most distasteful food and drink. The Psalmist may have thus described by figure what Christ found in reality (compare <reference osisRef="John.19.29">Joh 19:29</reference>, <reference osisRef="John.19.30">30</reference>). <div eID="gen9583" type="x-p"/>
entries.de204423dd233db62f7b0ab6ade2815f516e7272: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6264"/><div sID="gen9584" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6264"/>22-23. With unimportant verbal changes, this language is used by Paul to describe the rejection of the Jews who refused to receive the Saviour (<reference osisRef="Rom.11.9">Ro 11:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rom.11.10">10</reference>). The purport of the figures used is that blessings shall become curses, the "table" of joy (as one of food) a "snare," their<div eID="gen9584" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9585" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">welfare--</hi>literally, "peaceful condition," or security, a "trap." Darkened eyes and failing strength complete the picture of the ruin falling on them under the invoked retribution. <div eID="gen9585" type="x-p"/>
entries.3e142c08739232b3097fd43668b342a9c9f1909e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6266"/><div sID="gen9587" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6266"/><hi type="bold">24-25. An utter desolation awaits them. They will not only be driven from their homes, but their homes--</hi>or, literally, "palaces," indicative of wealth--shall be desolate (compare <reference osisRef="Matt.23.38">Mt 23:38</reference>). <div eID="gen9587" type="x-p"/>
entries.91a51fcc661bbe9d9473057424bb78b8fc33ca40: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6267"/><div sID="gen9588" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6267"/>26. Though smitten of God (<reference osisRef="Isa.53.4">Is 53:4</reference>), men were not less guilty in persecuting the sufferer (<reference osisRef="Acts.2.23">Ac 2:23</reference>).<div eID="gen9588" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9589" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">talk to the grief--</hi>in respect to, about it, implying derision and taunts.<div eID="gen9589" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9590" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">wounded--</hi>or, literally, "mortally wounded." <div eID="gen9590" type="x-p"/>
entries.3f11253fb1dd2bcc78fd62ba402d3c685b1ab3df: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6268"/><div sID="gen9591" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6268"/><hi type="bold">27-28. iniquity--</hi>or, "punishment of iniquity" (<reference osisRef="Ps.40.12">Psa 40:12</reference>).<div eID="gen9591" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9592" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">come ... righteousness--</hi>partake of its benefits. <div eID="gen9592" type="x-p"/>
entries.81e26692c73876e32821d5a80c8e69f753e87a34: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6270"/><div sID="gen9594" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6270"/><hi type="bold">29. poor and sorrowful--</hi>the afflicted pious, often denoted by such terms (compare <reference osisRef="Ps.10.17">Psa 10:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.12.5">12:5</reference>).<div eID="gen9594" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9595" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">set me ... high--</hi>out of danger. <div eID="gen9595" type="x-p"/>
entries.5ff4759af74cca1cee76f121fd1c2586f592c7e9: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6271"/><div sID="gen9596" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6271"/>30-31. Spiritual are better than mere material offerings (<reference osisRef="Ps.40.6">Psa 40:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.50.8">50:8</reference>); hence a promise of the former, and rather contemptuous terms are used of the latter. <div eID="gen9596" type="x-p"/>
entries.3abc7cf5b26c52d8cf324b3e7f35a9105504e647: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6272"/><div sID="gen9597" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6272"/>32-33. Others shall rejoice. "Humble" and poor, as in <reference osisRef="Ps.69.29">Psa 69:29</reference>.<div eID="gen9597" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9598" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">your heart, &c.--</hi>address to such (compare <reference osisRef="Ps.22.26">Psa 22:26</reference>). <div eID="gen9598" type="x-p"/>
entries.0148c0e3812b828cf4871b38702bb50edff36b70: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6274"/><div sID="gen9600" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6274"/>34-36. The call on the universe for praise is well sustained by the prediction of the perpetual and extended blessings which shall come upon the covenant-people of God. Though, as usual, the imagery is taken from terms used of Palestine, the whole tenor of the context indicates that the spiritual privileges and blessings of the Church are meant. <chapter eID="Ps.69"/>

entries.f5b4d020aae96bb2ea79726944faf17cab053d56: <div eID="gen20813" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen20814" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen20815" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen20815" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen20814" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen20816" type="x-p"/> The psalmist describes his afflicted state, and the wickedness of his adversaries, vv. 1-21; he declares the miseries that should come upon his enemies, <reference osisRef="Psa.69.22-Psa.69.28">Psa 69:22-28</reference>; enlarges on has afflicted state, and expresses his confidence in God, <reference osisRef="Psa.69.29-Psa.69.34">Psa 69:29-34</reference>; prophesies the restoration of the Jews to their own land and temple, <reference osisRef="Psa.69.35">Psa 69:35</reference>, <reference osisRef="Psa.69.36">Psa 69:36</reference>. <div eID="gen20816" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20817" type="x-p"/> The title is: "To the chief Musician upon Shoshannim, A Psalm of David." See this title explained on Psalm 45 (note). <div eID="gen20817" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20818" type="x-p"/> The Psalm is supposed to have been written during the captivity, and to have been the work of some Levite Divinely inspired. It is a very fine composition, equal to most in the Psalter. Several portions of it seem to have a reference to our Lord; to his advent passion, resurrection, the vocation of the Gentiles, the establishment of the Christian Church, and the reprobation of the Jews. The ninth verse is quoted by St. John, <reference osisRef="Joh.2.17">Joh 2:17</reference>. The twenty-first verse is quoted by St. Matthew, <reference osisRef="Mat.27.34">Mat 27:34</reference>, <reference osisRef="Mat.27.48">Mat 27:48</reference>; by St. Mark, <reference osisRef="Mar.15.23">Mar 15:23</reference>; by St. John, <reference osisRef="Joh.19.29">Joh 19:29</reference>; and applied to the sufferings of our Lord, in the treatment he received from the Jews. St. Paul quotes the twenty-second as a prophecy of the wickedness of the Jews, and the punishment they were to receive. He quotes the twenty-third verse in the same way. See <reference osisRef="Isa.6.9-Isa.6.10">Isa 6:9-10</reference> (note); <reference osisRef="Joh.12.39-Joh.12.40">Joh 12:39-40</reference> (note); <reference osisRef="Rom.11.10">Rom 11:10</reference> (note); <reference osisRef="2Cor.3.14">2Cor 3:14</reference> (note). Those portions which the writers of the New Testament apply to our Lord, we may apply also; of others we should be careful. <div eID="gen20818" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20819" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen20819" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20820" type="x-p"/> The waters are come in unto my soul - I am in the deepest distress. The waters have broken their dikes, and are just ready to sweep me away! Save me, Lord! In such circumstances I can have no other help. <div eID="gen20820" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20821" type="x-p"/> In the first, second, third, fourteenth, and fifteenth verses, the psalmist, speaking in the person of the captives in Babylon, compares their captivity to an abyss of waters, breaking all bounds, and ready to swallow them up; to a deep mire, in which there was no solid bottom, and no standing; and to a pot. in which they were about to be inclosed for ever. This is strongly figurative, and very expressive.
entries.e03f40f1e31db4e389833a9e50c918ec3fed9b45: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen20821" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20822" type="x-p"/> I am weary of my crying - A pathetic description of the state of the poor captives for about seventy years.
entries.d10c2dc15558abff628f04a13fe1a47449c10e18: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen20822" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20823" type="x-p"/> Then I restored that which I took not away - I think, with Calmet, that this is a sort of proverbial expression, like such as these, "Those who suffered the wrong, pay the costs." Delirant reges, plectuntur Achivi. "Kings sin, and the people are punished." "The fathers have eaten sour grapes, and the children's teeth are set on edge." Our fathers have grievously sinned against the Lord, and we their posterity suffer for it. See on <reference osisRef="Psa.69.12">Psa 69:12</reference> (note). Some have applied it to our Lord. I restored, by my suffering and death, that image of God and the Divine favor, which I took not away. That is, In my human nature I expiated the crime that human beings had committed against God. But such applications are very gratuitous.
entries.732e2dd164975a3787c85bc4af1d69bc94a44a69: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen20823" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20824" type="x-p"/> Thou knowest my foolishness - Though we have been brought into captivity in consequence of the crimes of our fathers, yet we have guilt enough of our own to merit a continuation of our miseries. How can such words as are in this verse be attributed to our blessed Lord, however they may be twisted or turned?
entries.d64251527a722242dad8e64aeef16c93572523a8: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen20824" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20825" type="x-p"/> Be ashamed for my sake - The sins of the Jews were a great stumbling-block in the way of the conversion of the Gentiles. They had been the peculiar people of the Lord. "How," say the Gentiles, "can a pure and holy Being love such people?" They were now punished for their crimes. "How," say the Gentiles, "can God deal so hardly with those whom he professes to love?" The pious among the captives felt keenly, because this reproach seemed to fall upon their gracious and merciful God.
entries.5724cc80c6927bbcc5bc8b67846d1a6faa2bf605: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen20825" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20826" type="x-p"/> For thy sake I have borne reproach - The Gentiles have said, "Why such an obstinate attachment to the worship of a Being who treats you so rigorously, and who interests not himself in your comfort and deliverance?" And in these cutting reproaches some of the ungodly Jews took a part: "I am an alien to my mother's children."
entries.5670a73a97f03d348ff2d32c8459c5641a3c5c05: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen20826" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20827" type="x-p"/> The zeal of thine house hath eaten me up - The strong desire to promote thy glory has absorbed all others. All the desires of my body and soul are wrapped up in this. This verse is very properly applied to our Lord, <reference osisRef="Joh.2.17">Joh 2:17</reference>, who went about doing good; and gave up his life, not only for the redemption of man, but to "magnify the law, and make it honorable."
entries.5c145fc5f2118cabfe8528c7af9beb8e0fa69065: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen20827" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20828" type="x-p"/> They that sit in the gate - At the gates were the courts for public justice; there were complaints lodged, and causes heard. No doubt many vexatious complaints were made against the poor captives; and false accusations, through which they grievously suffered; so that, literally, they were often "obliged to restore that which they had not taken away." See <reference osisRef="Psa.69.4">Psa 69:4</reference>. <div eID="gen20828" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20829" type="x-p"/> The song of the drunkards - These poor miserable people were exposed to all sorts of indignities. Though the conduct is base, the exultation over a fallen enemy is frequent. How miserable was this lot! Forsaken by friends, scorned by enemies, insulted by inferiors; the scoff of libertines, and the song of drunkards; besides hard travail of body, miserably lodged and fed; with the burning crown of all, a deep load of guilt upon the conscience. To such a life any death was preferable.
entries.22e49c8c0e7f223730f9cec2402730f39499fa78: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen20829" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20830" type="x-p"/> My prayer is unto thee, O Lord, in an acceptable time - This seems to refer to the end of the captivity, which Jeremiah had said should last seventy years, <reference osisRef="Jer.25.11">Jer 25:11</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.25.12">Jer 25:12</reference> : "The whole land shall be a desolation, and an astonishment; and these nations shall serve the king of Babylon seventy years. And it shall come to pass, when seventy years are accomplished, that I will punish the king of Babylon," etc. The conclusion of this period was the accepted tome of which the psalmist speaks. Now, they incessantly pray for the fulfillment of the promise made by Jeremiah: and to hear them, would be the truth of God's salvation; it would show the promise to be true, because the salvation - the deliverance, was granted.
entries.357bd1fa7425bed8ebda39e917f12501c686c7b0: <hi type="bold">Verse 16</hi> <div eID="gen20830" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20831" type="x-p"/> Thy loving-kindness is good - The word חסד chesed signifies exuberance of kindness, and the word רחמים rachamim, which we translate tender mercies, signifies such affection as mothers bear to their young: and in God, there is רב rob, a multitude, of such tender mercies towards the children of men!
entries.ef6beabecc022aa3685ca74f335deb95a8681217: <hi type="bold">Verse 18</hi> <div eID="gen20831" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20832" type="x-p"/> Deliver me because of mine enemies - Probably they now began to think that the redemption of these captives was not an impossible thing; that it was not far off; and therefore they had great rage, because they found their time was but short.
entries.95c0c135f5c8d849127bf990dc274b0c0e5c105d: <hi type="bold">Verse 19</hi> <div eID="gen20832" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20833" type="x-p"/> Thou hast known my reproach - This is one of the most forcible appeals to mercy and compassion that was ever made. The language of these two verses is inimitable; and the sentiment cannot be mended. I can devise no comment that would not lessen their effect.
entries.7a0401dec8f4277c96dd6a21f3f8a1d40cf745ef: <hi type="bold">Verse 21</hi> <div eID="gen20833" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20834" type="x-p"/> They gave me also gall for my meat - Even the food, necessary to preserve us in their slavery, was frequently mingled with what rendered it unpleasant and disgusting, though not absolutely unwholesome. And vinegar, sour small wines, was given us for our beverage. This is applied to our Lord, <reference osisRef="Mat.27.34">Mat 27:34</reference>, where the reader is requested to consult the notes.
entries.1f53bcf25c30fee5f53c2889a30a554877396c35: <hi type="bold">Verse 22</hi> <div eID="gen20834" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20835" type="x-p"/> Let their table become a snare - The execrations here and in the following verses should be read in the future tense, because they are predictive; and not in the imperative mood, as if they were the offspring of the psalmist's resentment: "Their table Shall become a snare; - their eyes Shall be darkened; - thou Wilt pour out thine indignation upon them; - thy wrathful anger Shall take hold of them; - their habitation Shall be desolate, - and none Shall dwell in their tents." <div eID="gen20835" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20836" type="x-p"/> The psalmist prophesies that the evils which they had inflicted on the Israelites should be visited on themselves; that as they had made them eat, drink, labor, and suffer, so God should in his judgment treat them.
entries.141a18a54db70a0011d3c276a3bb1aeefa4f03e5: <hi type="bold">Verse 27</hi> <div eID="gen20836" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20837" type="x-p"/> Add iniquity unto their iniquity - תנה עון על עונם tenah avon al avonam; give iniquity, that is, the reward of it, upon or for their iniquity. Or, as the original signifies perverseness, treat their perverseness with perverseness: act, in thy judgments, as crookedly towards them as they dealt crookedly towards thee. They shall get, in the way of punishment, what they have dealt out in the way of oppression.
entries.0732f8d4abf99ea87c3f11f9eec86bda96b9805f: <hi type="bold">Verse 28</hi> <div eID="gen20837" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20838" type="x-p"/> Let them be blotted out - They shall be blotted out from the land of the living. They shall be cut off from life, which they have forfeited by their cruelty and oppression. The psalmist is speaking of retributive justice; and in this sense all these passages are to be understood. <div eID="gen20838" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20839" type="x-p"/> And not be written with the righteous - They shall have no title to that long life which God has promised to his followers.
entries.dcf4d475bf15314d8af69aa495b05b3dad3a07d5: <hi type="bold">Verse 29</hi> <div eID="gen20839" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20840" type="x-p"/> I am poor and sorrowful - Literally, I an laid low, and full of pain or grief. Hence the prayer, "Let thy salvation, O God set me on high!" My oppression has laid me low; thy salvation shall make me high!
entries.d555cd4d028d84825731540c7345cc93f1ae44f4: <hi type="bold">Verse 31</hi> <div eID="gen20840" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20841" type="x-p"/> An ox or bullock that hath horns and hoofs - Oxen offered in sacrifice had their horns and hoofs gilded; and the psalmist might mention these parts of the victim more particularly, because they were more conspicuous. Others think that full-grown animals are intended, those that had perfect horns, in opposition to calves or steers. I think the first the preferable sense; for the horns, etc., of consecrated animals are thus ornamented in the east to the present day.
entries.30320022568078bc6144f21ef3ef848970f0df79: <hi type="bold">Verse 32</hi> <div eID="gen20841" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20842" type="x-p"/> The humble shall see this, and be glad - Those who are low, pressed down by misfortune or cruelty, shall see this and take courage; expecting that thou wilt lift them up also; and thus the heart of those who seek the Lord shall be revived.
entries.c46e0fd4fafd285a864f106dd6b8e42d4ccee9ea: <hi type="bold">Verse 33</hi> <div eID="gen20842" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20843" type="x-p"/> For the Lord heareth the poor - אביונים ebyonim, of the beggars. He perhaps refers here to the case of the captives, many of whom were reduced to the most abject state, so as to be obliged to beg bread from their heathen oppressors. <div eID="gen20843" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20844" type="x-p"/> His prisoners - The captives, shut up by his judgments in Chaldea, without any civil liberty, like culprits in a prison.
entries.3aa391d80664006c98f1b83784f73c6545bc2b92: <hi type="bold">Verse 34</hi> <div eID="gen20844" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20845" type="x-p"/> Let the heaven and earth praise him - The psalmist has the fullest confidence that God will turn their captivity, and therefore calls upon all creatures to magnify him for his mercy.
entries.1c5b8f0bd9d8f6d201777a593fb372fefa383ba3: <hi type="bold">Verse 35</hi> <div eID="gen20845" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20846" type="x-p"/> God will save Zion - This fixes the Psalm to the time of the captivity. There was no Zion belonging to the Jews in the time of Saul, when those suppose the Psalm to be written who make David the author; for David after he came to the throne, won the stronghold of Zion from the Jebusites. <reference osisRef="2Sam.5.7">2Sam 5:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Chr.11.5">1Chr 11:5</reference>. <div eID="gen20846" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20847" type="x-p"/> Will build the cities of Judah - This refers to the return from the captivity, when all the destroyed cities should be rebuilt, and the Jews repossess their forfeited heritages. Some apply this to the redemption of the human race; and suppose that Zion is the type of the Christian Church into which the Gentiles were to be called. What evangelists and apostles apply to our Lord, we safely may. What others see so clearly in this Psalm relative to Gospel matters, I cannot discern.  <chapter eID="Ps.69"/> <div eID="gen20847" type="x-p"/>

entries.912ea324829036d6be70502a5b42d0daa2b64bbe: <reference osisRef="Ps.69.1-Ps.69.13">Psa 69:1-13</reference> <div eID="gen9695" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9696" type="x-p"/> Out of deep distress, the work of his foes, the complaining one cries for help; he thinks upon his sins, which is sufferings bring to his remembrance, but he is also distinctly conscious that he is an object of scorn and hostility for God’s sake, and from His mercy he looks for help in accordance with His promises.
