The waters are said to rush in unto the soul (עד־נפשׁ), when they so press upon the imperilled one that the soul, i.e., the life of the body, more especially the breath, is threatened; cf. <reference osisRef="Jonah.2.6">Jon 2:6</reference>; Jer 4:10. Waters are also a figure of calamities that come on like a flood and drag one into their vortex, <reference osisRef="Ps.18.17">Psa 18:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.32.6">Psa 32:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.124.5">Psa 124:5</reference>, cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.66.12">Psa 66:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.88.8">Psa 88:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.88.18">Psa 88:18</reference>; here, however, the figure is cut off in such a way that it conveys the impression of reality expressed in a poetical form, as in Ps 40, and much the same as in Jonah’s psalm. The soft, yielding morass is called יון, and the eddying deep מצוּלה. The <hi type="italic">Nomen Hophal</hi>. מעמד signifies properly a being placed, then a standing-place, or firm standing (lxx ὑπόστασις), like מטּה, that which is stretched out, extension, Isa 8:8. שׁבּלת (Ephraimitish סבּלת) is a streaming, a flood, from שׁבל, Arab. <hi type="italic">sbl</hi>, to stream, flow (cf. note on <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.58.9">Psa 58:9</reference></hi>). בּוא בּ, to fall into, as in <reference osisRef="Ps.66.12">Psa 66:12</reference>, and שׁטף with an accusative, to overflow, as in Psa 124:4. The complaining one is nearly drowned in consequence of his sinking down, for he has long cried in vain for help: he is wearied by continual crying (יגע בּ, as in <reference osisRef="Ps.6.7">Psa 6:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.45.3">Jer 45:3</reference>), his throat is parched (נחר from חרר; lxx and Jerome: it is become hoarse), his eyes have failed (<reference osisRef="Jer.14.6">Jer 14:6</reference>) him, who waits upon his God. The participle מיחל, equal to a relative clause, is, as in 18:51, 1Ki 14:6, attached to the suffix of the preceding noun (Hitzig). Distinct from this use of the participle without the article is the adverbially qualifying participle in <reference osisRef="Gen.3.8">Gen 3:8</reference>; Sol 5:2, cf. חי,   <reference osisRef="2Sam.12.21">2Sa 12:21</reference>; 2Sa 18:14. There is no necessity for the correction of the text מיּחל (lxx apo' τοῦ elpi'zein me). Concerning the accentuation of רבּוּ vid., on Psa 38:20. Apart from the words “more than the hairs of my head” (<reference osisRef="Ps.40.13">Psa 40:13</reference>), the complaint of the multitude of groundless enemies is just the same as in <reference osisRef="Ps.38.20">Psa 38:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.35.19">Psa 35:19</reference>, cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.109.3">Psa 109:3</reference>, both in substance and expression. Instead of מצמיתי, my destroyers, the Syriac version has the reading מעצמותי (more numerous than my bones), which is approved by Hupfeld; but to reckon the multitude of the enemy by the number of one’s own bones is both devoid of taste and unheard of. Moreover the reading of our text finds support, if it need any, in Lam 3:52. The words, “what I have not taken away, I must then restore,” are intended by way of example, and perhaps, as also in <reference osisRef="Jer.15.10">Jer 15:10</reference>, as a proverbial expression: that which I have not done wrong, I must suffer for (cf. <reference osisRef="Jer.15.10">Jer 15:10</reference>, and the similar complaint in <reference osisRef="Ps.35.11">Psa 35:11</reference>). One is tempted to take אז in the sense of “nevertheless” (Ewald), a meaning, however, which it is by no means intended to convey. In this passage it takes the place of זאת (cf. οὕτως for ταῦτα, <reference osisRef="Matt.7.12">Mat 7:12</reference>), inasmuch as it gives prominence to the restitution desired, as an inference from a false assumption: then, although I took it not away, stole it not. <div eID="gen9696" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9697" type="x-p"/> The transition from the bewailing of suffering to a confession of sin is like Psa 40:13. In the undeserved persecution which he endures at the hand of man, he is obliged nevertheless to recognise well-merited chastisement from the side of God. And whilst by אתּה ידעתּ (cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.40.10">Psa 40:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.15.15">Jer 15:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.17.16">Jer 17:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.18.23">Jer 18:23</reference>, and on ל as an exponent of the object, <reference osisRef="Jer.16.16">Jer 16:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.40.2">Jer 40:2</reference>) he does not acknowledge himself to be a sinner after the standard of his own shortsightedness, but of the divine omniscience, he at the same time commends his sinful need, which with self-accusing modesty he calls אוּלת (<reference osisRef="Ps.38.6">Psa 38:6</reference>) and אשׁמות    (<reference osisRef="2Chr.28.10">2Ch 28:10</reference>), to the mercy of the omniscient One. Should he, the sinner, be abandoned by God to destruction, then all those who are faithful in their intentions towards the Lord would be brought to shame and confusion in him, inasmuch as they would be taunted with this example. קויך designates the godly from the side of the πίστις, and מבקשׁיךa from the side of the ἀγάπη. The multiplied names of God are so many appeals to God’s honour, to the truthfulness of His covenant relationship. The person praying here is, it is true, a sinner, but that is no justification of the conduct of men towards him; he is suffering for the Lord’s sake, and it is the Lord Himself who is reviled in him. It is upon this he bases his prayer in Psa 69:8. עליך, for thy sake, as in <reference osisRef="Ps.44.23">Psa 44:23</reference>; Jer 15:15. The reproach that he has to bear, and ignominy that has covered his face and made it quite unrecognisable (<reference osisRef="Ps.44.16">Psa 44:16</reference>, cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.83.17">Psa 83:17</reference>), have totally estranged (<reference osisRef="Ps.38.12">Psa 38:12</reference>, cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.88.9">Psa 88:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="Job.19.13-Job.19.15">Job 19:13-15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.12.6">Jer 12:6</reference>) from him even his own brethren (אחי, parallel word בּני אמּי, as in <reference osisRef="Ps.50.20">Psa 50:20</reference>; cf. on the other hand, <reference osisRef="Gen.49.8">Gen 49:8</reference>, where the interchange designedly takes another form of expression); for the glow of his zeal (קנאהּ from קנא, according to the Arabic, to be a deep or bright red) for the house of Jahve, viz., for the sanctity of the sanctuary and of the congregation gathered about it (which is never directly called “the house of Jahve” in the Old Testament, vid., Köhler on Zec 9:8, but here, as in Num 12:7; Hos 8:1, is so called in conjunction with the sanctuary), as also for the honour of His who sits enthroned therein, consumes him, like a fire burning in his bones which incessantly breaks forth and rages all through him (<reference osisRef="Jer.20.9">Jer 20:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.23.9">Jer 23:9</reference>), and therefore all the malice of those who are estranged from God is concentrated upon and against him. <div eID="gen9697" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9698" type="x-p"/> He now goes on to describe how sorrow for the sad condition of the house of God has brought noting but reproach to him (cf. Psa 109:24.). It is doubtful whether נפשׁי is an alternating subject to ואבכּה (<hi type="italic">fut. consec</hi>. without being apocopated), cf. <reference osisRef="Jer.13.17">Jer 13:17</reference>, or a more minutely defining accusative as in <reference osisRef="Isa.26.9">Isa 26:9</reference> (vid., on <reference osisRef="Ps.3.5">Psa 3:5</reference>), or whether, together with בּצּום, it forms a circumstantial clause (<hi type="italic">et flevi dum in jejunio esset anima mea</hi>), or even whether it is intended to be taken as an accusative of the object in a pregnant construction (= בּכה ושׁפך נפשׁו, <reference osisRef="Ps.42.5">Psa 42:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Sam.1.15">1Sa 1:15</reference>): I wept away my soul in fasting. Among all these possible renderings, the last is the least probable, and the first, according to <reference osisRef="Ps.44.3">Psa 44:3</reference>; 83:19, by far the most probable, and also that which is assumed by the accentuation.<note placement="foot">The <hi type="italic">Munach</hi> of בצום is a transformation of <hi type="italic">Dechî</hi> (just as the <hi type="italic">Munach</hi> of לחרפות is a transformation of <hi type="italic">Mugrash</hi>), in connection with which נקשי might certainly be conceived of even as object (cf. <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.26.6">Psa 26:6</reference></hi>); but this after ואבכּה (not ואבכּה), and as being without example, could hardly have entered the minds of the punctuists.</note> <div eID="gen9698" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9699" type="x-p"/> The reading of the lxx ואענּה, καὶ συνέκαψα (Olshausen, Hupfeld, and Böttcher), is a very natural (<reference osisRef="Ps.35.13">Psa 35:13</reference>) exchange of the poetically bold expression for one less choice and less expressive (since ענּה נפשׁ is a phrase of the Pentateuch equivalent to צוּם). The garb of mourning, like the fasting, is an expression of sorrow for public distresses, not, as in <reference osisRef="Ps.35.13">Psa 35:13</reference>, of personal condolence; concerning ואתּנה, vid., on Psa 3:6. On account of this mourning, reproach after reproach comes upon him, and they fling gibes and raillery at him; everywhere, both in the gate, the place where the judges sit and where business is transacted, and also at carousals, he is jeered at and traduced (<reference osisRef="Lam.3.14">Lam 3:14</reference>, cf. <reference osisRef="Lam.5.14">Lam 5:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.30.9">Job 30:9</reference>). שׂיח בּ signifies in itself <hi type="italic">fabulari de...</hi> without any bad secondary meaning (cf. <reference osisRef="Prov.6.22">Pro 6:22</reference>, <hi type="italic">confabulabitur tecum</hi>); here it is construed first with a personal and then a neuter subject (cf. <reference osisRef="Amos.8.3">Amo 8:3</reference>), for in <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.69.13">Psa 69:13</reference></hi> neither הייתי (<reference osisRef="Job.30.9">Job 30:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Lam.3.14">Lam 3:14</reference>) nor אני (<reference osisRef="Lam.3.63">Lam 3:63</reference>) is to be supplied. <reference osisRef="Ps.69.14">Psa 69:14</reference> tells us how he acts in the face of such hatred and scorn; ואני, as in <reference osisRef="Ps.109.4">Psa 109:4</reference>, <hi type="italic">sarcasmis hostium suam opponit in precibus constantiam </hi>(Geier). As for himself, his prayer is directed towards Jahve at the present time, when his affliction as a witness for God gives him the assurance that He will be well-pleased to accept it (עת רצון = בעת רצון, <reference osisRef="Isa.49.8">Isa 49:8</reference>). It is addressed to Him who is at the same time <hi type="italic">Jahve</hi> and <hi type="italic">Elohim</hi>, - the revealed One in connection with the history of redemption, and the absolute One in His exaltation above the world, - on the ground of the greatness and fulness of His mercy: may He then answer him with or in the truth of His salvation, i.e., the infallibility with which His purpose of mercy verifies itself in accordance with the promises given. Thus is <reference osisRef="Ps.69.14">Psa 69:14</reference> to be explained in accordance with the accentuation. According to <reference osisRef="Isa.49.8">Isa 49:8</reference>, it looks as though עת רצון must be drawn to ענני (Hitzig), but <reference osisRef="Ps.32.6">Psa 32:6</reference> sets us right on this point; and the fact that ברב־חסדך is joined to <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.69.14">Psa 69:14</reference></hi> also finds support from Psa 5:8. But the repetition of the divine name perplexes one, and it may be asked whether or not the accent that divides the verse into its two parts might not more properly stand beside רצון, as in <reference osisRef="Ps.32.6">Psa 32:6</reference> beside מצא; so that <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.69.14">Psa 69:14</reference></hi> runs: <hi type="italic">Elohim, by virtue of the greatness of Thy mercy hear me, by virtue of the truth of Thy salvation.  </hi>
entries.02f576e896f3915d8cad2f93ae44731f24d429b1: <reference osisRef="Ps.69.14-Ps.69.21">Psa 69:14-21</reference> <div eID="gen9699" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9700" type="x-p"/> In this second part the petition by which the first is as it were encircled, is continued; the peril grows greater the longer it lasts, and with it the importunity of the cry for help. The figure of sinking in the mire or mud and in the depths of the pit (בּאר, Ps 55:24, cf. בור, <reference osisRef="Ps.40.3">Psa 40:3</reference>) is again taken up, and so studiously wrought out, that the impression forces itself upon one that the poet is here describing something that has really taken place. The combination “from those who hate me and from the depths of the waters” shows that “the depths of the waters” is not a merely rhetorical figure; and the form of the prayer: let not the pit (the well-pit or covered tank) close (תּאטּר with Dagesh in the Teth, in order to guard against its being read תּאטר; cf. on the signification of אטּר, <hi type="italic">clausus = claudus</hi>, scil. <hi type="italic">manu</hi>) its mouth (i.e., its upper opening) upon me, exceeds the limits of anything that can be allowed to mere rhetoric. “Let not the water-flood overflow me” is intended to say, since it has, according to <reference osisRef="Ps.69.3">Psa 69:3</reference>, already happened, let it not go further to my entire destruction. The “answer me” in <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.69.17">Psa 69:17</reference></hi> is based upon the plea that God’s loving-kindness is טּוב, i.e., good, absolutely good (as in the kindred passion-Psalm, <reference osisRef="Ps.109.21">Psa 109:21</reference>), better than all besides (<reference osisRef="Ps.63.4">Psa 63:4</reference>), the means of healing or salvation from all evil. On <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.69.17">Psa 69:17</reference></hi> cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.51.3">Psa 51:3</reference>, Lam 3:32. In <reference osisRef="Ps.69.18">Psa 69:18</reference> the prayer is based upon the painful situation of the poet, which urgently calls for speedy help (מהר beside the imperative, <reference osisRef="Ps.102.3">Psa 102:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.143.7">Psa 143:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gen.19.22">Gen 19:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Esth.6.10">Est 6:10</reference>, is certainly itself not an imperative like הרב, <reference osisRef="Ps.51.4">Psa 51:4</reference>, but an adverbial infinitive as in <reference osisRef="Ps.79.8">Psa 79:8</reference>). קרבה, or, in order to ensure the pronunciation <hi type="italic">ḳorbah</hi> in distinction from <hi type="italic">ḳārbah</hi>, <reference osisRef="Deut.15.9">Deu 15:9</reference>, קרבה (in Baer,<note placement="foot">Originally - was the sign for every kind of o6, hence the Masora includes the חטוף also under the name קמץ חטף; vid., <hi type="italic">Luther. Zeitschrift</hi>, 1863, S. 412,f., cf. Wright, <hi type="italic">Genesis</hi>, p. xxix.)</note> is <hi type="italic">imperat. Kal</hi>; cf. the fulfilment in Lam 3:57. The reason assigned, “because of mine enemies,” as in <reference osisRef="Ps.5.9">Psa 5:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.27.11">Psa 27:11</reference>, and frequently, is to be understood according to <reference osisRef="Ps.13.5">Psa 13:5</reference> : the honour of the all-holy One cannot suffer the enemies of the righteous to triumph over him.<note placement="foot">Both נפשׁי and איבי, contrary to logical interpunction, are marked with <hi type="italic">Munach</hi>; the former ought properly to have <hi type="italic">Dechî</hi>, and the latter <hi type="italic">Mugrash</hi>. But since neither the <hi type="italic">Athnach</hi>-word nor the <hi type="italic">Silluk</hi>-word has two syllables preceding the tone syllable, the accents are transformed according to <hi type="italic">Accentuationssystem</hi>, xviii. §2, 4.</note> <div eID="gen9700" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9701" type="x-p"/> The accumulation of synonyms in <reference osisRef="Ps.69.20">Psa 69:20</reference> is Jeremiah’s custom, <reference osisRef="Jer.13.14">Jer 13:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.21.5">Jer 21:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.21.7">Jer 21:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.32.37">Jer 32:37</reference>, and is found also in Ps 31 (<reference osisRef="Ps.31.10">Psa 31:10</reference>) and Ps 44 (<reference osisRef="Ps.44.4">Psa 44:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.44.17">Psa 44:17</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.44.25">Psa 44:25</reference>). On הרפּה שׁברה לבּי, cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.51.19">Psa 51:19</reference>, Jer 23:9. The ἅπαξ γεγραμ, ואנוּשׁה (historical tense), from נוּשׁ, is explained by ענוּשׁ from אנשׁ, sickly, dangerously ill, evil-disposed, which is a favourite word in Jeremiah. Moreover נוּד in the signification of manifesting pity, not found elsewhere in the Psalter, is common in Jeremiah, e.g., <reference osisRef="Ps.15.5">Psa 15:5</reference>; it signifies originally to nod to any one as a sign of a pity that sympathizes with him and recognises the magnitude of the evil. “To give wormwood for meat and מי־ראשׁ to drink” is a Jeremianic (<reference osisRef="Jer.8.14">Jer 8:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.9.14">Jer 9:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.23.15">Jer 23:15</reference>) designation for inflicting the extreme of pain and anguish upon one. ראשׁ (רושׁ) signifies first of all a poisonous plant with an umbellated head of flower or a capitate fruit; but then, since bitter and poisonous are interchangeable notions in the Semitic languages, it signifies gall as the bitterest of the bitter. The lxx renders: καὶ ἔδωκαν εἰς τὸ βρῶμά μου χολήν, καὶ εἰς τὴν δίψαν μου ἐπότισάν με ὄξος. Certainly נתן בּ can mean to put something into something, to mix something with it, but the parallel word לצמאי (for my thirst, i.e., for the quenching of it, <reference osisRef="Neh.9.15">Neh 9:15</reference>, <reference osisRef="Neh.9.20">Neh 9:20</reference>) favours the supposition that the בּ of בּברוּתי is <hi type="italic">Beth essentiae</hi>, after which Luther renders: “they give me gall to eat.” The ἅπαξ γεγραμ. בּרוּת (<reference osisRef="Lam.4.10">Lam 4:10</reference> בּרות) signifies βρῶσις, from בּרה, βιβρώσκειν (root βορ, Sanscrit gar, Latin <hi type="italic">vor-are</hi>).
entries.119a08be3e9044bd7a0aa1d9b978beefe91052ae: <reference osisRef="Ps.69.22-Ps.69.36">Psa 69:22-36</reference> <div eID="gen9701" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9702" type="x-p"/> The description of the suffering has reached its climax in <reference osisRef="Ps.69.22">Psa 69:22</reference>, at which the wrath of the persecuted one flames up and bursts forth in imprecations. The first imprecation joins itself upon Psa 69:22. They have given the sufferer gall and vinegar; therefore their table, which was abundantly supplied, is to be turned into a snare to them, from which they shall not be able to escape, and that לפניהם, in the very midst of their banqueting, whilst the table stands spread out before them (<reference osisRef="Ezek.23.41">Eze 23:41</reference>). שׁלומים (collateral form of שׁלמים) is the name given to them as being carnally secure; the word signifies the peaceable or secure in a good (<reference osisRef="Ps.55.21">Psa 55:21</reference>) and in a bad sense. Destruction is to overtake them suddenly, “when they say: Peace and safety” (<reference osisRef="1Thess.5.3">1Th 5:3</reference>). The lxx erroneously renders: καὶ εἰς ἀνταπόδοσιν = וּלשׁלּוּמים. The association of ideas in <reference osisRef="Ps.69.24">Psa 69:24</reference> is transparent. With their eyes they have feasted themselves upon the sufferer, and in the strength of their loins they have ill-treated him. These eyes with their bloodthirsty malignant looks are to grow blind. These loins full of defiant self-confidence are to shake (המעד, <hi type="italic">imperat.</hi> <hi type="italic">Hiph</hi>. like הרחק, <reference osisRef="Job.13.21">Job 13:21</reference>, from המעיד, for which in <reference osisRef="Ezek.29.7">Eze 29:7</reference>, and perhaps also in <reference osisRef="Dan.11.14">Dan 11:14</reference>, we find העמיד). Further: God is to pour out His wrath upon them (<reference osisRef="Ps.79.6">Psa 79:6</reference>; Hos 5:10; <reference osisRef="Jer.10.25">Jer 10:25</reference>), i.e., let loose against them the cosmical forces of destruction existing originally in His nature. זעמּך has the <hi type="italic">Dagesh</hi> in order to distinguish it in pronunciation from זעמך. In <reference osisRef="Ps.69.26">Psa 69:26</reference> טירה (from טוּר, to encircle) is a designation of an encamping or dwelling-place (lxx ἔπαυλις) taken from the circular encampments (Arabic <hi type="italic">ṣı̂rât , ṣirât</hi>, and <hi type="italic">dwâr , duâr</hi>) of the nomads (<reference osisRef="Gen.25.16">Gen 25:16</reference>). The laying waste and desolation of his own house is the most fearful of all misfortunes to the Semite (<hi type="italic">Job</hi>, note to <reference osisRef="Ps.18.15">Psa 18:15</reference>). The poet derives the justification of such fearful imprecations from the fact that they persecute him, who is besides smitten of God. God has smitten him on account of his sins, and that by having placed him in the midst of a time in which he must be consumed with zeal and solicitude for the house of God. The suffering decreed for him by God is therefore at one and the same time suffering as a chastisement and as a witnessing for God; and they heighten this suffering by every means in their power, not manifesting any pity for him or any indulgence, but imputing to him sins that he has not committed, and requiting him with deadly hatred for benefits for which they owed him thanks. <div eID="gen9702" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9703" type="x-p"/> There are also some others, although but few, who share this martyrdom with him. The psalmist calls them, as he looks up to Jahve, חלליך, Thy fatally smitten ones; they are those to whom God has appointed that they should bear within themselves a pierced or wounded heart (vid., <reference osisRef="Ps.109.22">Psa 109:22</reference>, cf. <reference osisRef="Jer.8.18">Jer 8:18</reference>) in the face of such a godless age. Of the deep grief (אל, as in <reference osisRef="Ps.2.7">Psa 2:7</reference>) of these do they tell, viz., with self-righteous, self-blinded mockery (cf. the Talmudic phrase ספר בלשׁון הרע or ספר לשׁון הרע, of evil report or slander). The lxx and Syriac render יוסיפוּ (προσέθηκαν): they add to the anguish; the Targum, Aquila, Symmachus, and Jerome follow the traditional text. Let God therefore, by the complete withdrawal of His grace, suffer them to fall from one sin into another - this is the meaning of the <hi type="italic">da culpam super culpam eorum</hi> - in order that accumulated judgment may correspond to the accumulated guilt (<reference osisRef="Jer.16.18">Jer 16:18</reference>). Let the entrance into God’s righteousness, i.e., His justifying and sanctifying grace, be denied to them for ever. Let them be blotted out of ספר חיּים (<reference osisRef="Exod.32.32">Exo 32:32</reference>, cf. <reference osisRef="Isa.4.3">Isa 4:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Dan.12.1">Dan 12:1</reference>), that is to say, struck out of the list of the living, and that of the living in this present world; for it is only in the New Testament that we meet with the Book of Life as a list of the names of the heirs of the ζωὴ αἰώνιος. According to the conception both of the Old and of the New Testament the צדיקים are the heirs of life. Therefore <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.69.29">Psa 69:29</reference></hi> wishes that they may not be written by the side of the righteous, who, according to <reference osisRef="Hab.2.4">Hab 2:4</reference>, “live,” i.e., are preserved, by their faith. With ואני the poet contrasts himself, as in Ps 40:18, with those deserving of execration. They are now on high, but in order to be brought low; he is miserable and full of poignant pain, but in order to be exalted; God’s salvation will remove him from his enemies on to a height that is too steep for them (<reference osisRef="Ps.59.2">Psa 59:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.91.14">Psa 91:14</reference>). Then will he praise (הלּל) and magnify (גּדּל) the Name of God with song and thankful confession. And such spiritual תּודה, such thank-offering of the heart, is more pleasing to God than an ox, a bullock, i.e., a young ox (= פּר השּׁור, an ox-bullock, Jdg 6:25, according to Ges. §113), one having horns and a cloven hoof (Ges. §53, 2). The attributives do not denote the rough material animal nature (Hengstenberg), but their legal qualifications for being sacrificed. מקרין is the name for the young ox as not being under three years old (cf. <reference osisRef="1Sam.1.24">1Sa 1:24</reference>, lxx ἐν μόσχῳ τριετίζοντι); מפריס as belonging to the clean four-footed animals, viz., those that are cloven-footed and chew the cud, Lev. 11. Even the most stately, full-grown, clean animal that may be offered as a sacrifice stands in the sight of Jahve very far below the sacrifice of grateful praise coming from the heart. <div eID="gen9703" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9704" type="x-p"/> When now the patient sufferers (ענוים) united with the poet by community of affliction shall see how he offers the sacrifice of thankful confession, they will rejoice. ראוּ is a hypothetical preterite; it is neither וראוּ (<hi type="italic">perf. consec</hi>.), nor יראוּ (<reference osisRef="Ps.40.4">Psa 40:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.52.8">Psa 52:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.107.42">Psa 107:42</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.22.19">Job 22:19</reference>). The declaration conveying information to be expected in <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.69.33">Psa 69:33</reference></hi> after the <hi type="italic">Waw apodoseos</hi> changes into an apostrophe of the “seekers of Elohim:” their heart shall revive, for, as they have suffered in company with him who is now delivered, they shall now also refresh themselves with him. We are at once reminded of <reference osisRef="Ps.22.27">Psa 22:27</reference>, where this is as it were the exhortation of the entertainer at the thank-offering meal. It would be rash to read שׁמע in <reference osisRef="Ps.69.23">Psa 69:23</reference>, after <reference osisRef="Ps.22.25">Psa 22:25</reference>, instead of שׁמע (Olshausen); the one object in that passage is here generalized: Jahve is attentive to the needy, and doth not despise His bound ones (<reference osisRef="Ps.107.10">Psa 107:10</reference>), but, on the contrary, He takes an interest in them and helps them. Starting from this proposition, which is the clear gain of that which has been experienced, the view of the poet widens into the prophetic prospect of the bringing back of Israel out of the Exile into the Land of Promise. In the face of this fact of redemption of the future he calls upon (cf. <reference osisRef="Isa.44.23">Isa 44:23</reference>) all created things to give praise to God, who will bring about the salvation of Zion, will build again the cities of Judah, and restore the land, freed from its desolation, to the young God-fearing generation, the children of the servants of God among the exiles. The feminine suffixes refer to ערי (cf. <reference osisRef="Jer.2.15">Jer 2:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.22.6">Jer 22:6</reference> <hi type="italic">Chethîb</hi>). The tenor of <reference osisRef="Isa.65.9">Isa 65:9</reference> is similar. If the Psalm were written by David, the closing turn from <reference osisRef="Ps.69.23">Psa 69:23</reference> onwards might be more difficult of comprehension than <reference osisRef="Ps.14.7">Psa 14:7</reference>; 51:20f. If, however, it is by Jeremiah, then we do not need to persuade ourselves that it is to be understood not of restoration and re-peopling, but of continuance and completion (Hofmann and Kurtz). Jeremiah lived to experience the catastrophe he foretold; but the nearer it came to the time, the more comforting were the words with which he predicted the termination of the Exile and the restoration of Israel. <reference osisRef="Jer.34.7">Jer 34:7</reference> shows us how natural to him, and to him in particular, was the distinction between Jerusalem and the cities of Judah. The predictions in <reference osisRef="Jer.32.1">Jer 32:1</reference>, which sound so in accord with Psa 69:36., belong to the time of the second siege. Jerusalem was not yet fallen; the strong places of the land, however, already lay in ruins.  <chapter eID="Ps.69"/> <div eID="gen9704" type="x-p"/>

PSALM 69
There is a close resemblance between this psalm and the twenty-second. In the opening verses, David complains of the barbarous cruelty of his enemies, and of the grievous wrongs which they had inflicted upon him.
The particular enemies of whom he speaks are uncertain; some referring the occasion of the composition of the psalm to his persecution by Saul, and others to the rebellion of Absalom. But to whatever part of David’s eventful life the psalm primarily refers, it may be concluded, from the frequency with which it is quoted and applied to Christ in the New Testament, that it was prophetic of him, of whom David, rejected and persecuted, was an eminent type. It is quoted in the New Testament at least seven times; the 4th verse in John 15:25; the 9th verse in John 2:17, and Romans 15:3; the 21st verse in Matthew 27:34, 48, and John 19:28, 29; the 22d and 23d verses in Romans 11:9, 10; and the 25th verse in Acts 1:16, 20.
But his mind, he affirms, was not hereby reduced to such a state of distress as to prevent him from patiently relying on the protection of God, or to discourage him from continuing in the undeviating course of a holy and an upright life. He rather testifies that his piety, and the courage and activity which he had manifested in maintaining the interests of the divine glory, were the cause of the hostility borne to him by the generality of men. After having again complained of being not less shamefully than cruelly oppressed by his enemies, he invokes God to visit them with deserved punishment. In the close, exulting as if he had obtained his highest wishes, he engages to yield to God a solemn sacrifice of praise.
To the chief musician upon Shoshannim of David.
We have already spoken elsewhere of the word Shoshannim. Its proper meaning is uncertain and obscure; but the most probable conjecture is, that it was the commencement of some song. If, however, any would prefer considering it as the name of some musical instrument, I have no objections. But the opinion held by some that this psalm was composed at the season of spring, when the lilies begin to blossom, is altogether unfounded and frivolous.
They rest this opinion upon the meaning which they attach to the word ששנים, Shoshannim, in the title of the psalm, which they translate lilies
Before proceeding farther, we would have you to observe that David wrote this inspired ode not so much in his own name, as in the name of the whole Church, of whose Head he was an eminent type, as will be more dearly brought out in the sequel. This is highly worthy of our notice, that from this consideration we may be led to contemplate with the greater attention the representation which is here given of the common condition of all the people of God. Besides, it is highly probable that David did not here comprehend only one kind of persecution, but all the evils which he had suffered during the course of many years.
Psalm 69:1-5
1. Save me, O God! for the waters have entered in unto my soul. 2. I am sunk in deep mire, where there is no footing, [or standing place:] I am come into deep waters, and the flood
“Ou, la force et le fil.” — Fr. marg. “Or, the force and course.”
of the water overfloweth me. 3. I am weary of crying; my throat has become hoarse therewith: my eyes have failed with [or in] waiting for my God. 4. They who hate me without cause are more in number than the hairs of my head: my lying adversaries, who eagerly desire to destroy me, are increased;
“Ou, fortifiez.” — Fr. marg. “Or, strengthened.”
that which I took not by spoil, then
The Hebrew word אז, for then, appears to be emphatic. “אז; in ipso articulo, (Schultens in Proverbs 7:22;) immediately, without any contention, or delay.” Lowth, quoted in Merrick’s Annotations.
I restored it. 5. O God! thou knowest my foolishness; and my faults are not hidden from thee.
 
1. Save me, O God! for the waters, etc. Under the figure of waters, the Psalmist represents his condition as so extremely distressing that it brought him even to the brink of despair; and yet we know that, so far from being a soft and an effeminate person, he was one who encountered and overcame dreadful temptations with extraordinary courage. Whence we may infer the bitterness of the distress with which he was at that time afflicted. Some understand the word soul as denoting life;
“The waters are come in unto my soul; i.e., a flood of overwhelming calamities threaten my life: comp. verse 16.” — Cresswell. Williams thinks the allusion is to a leaky vessel, or to an inundation.
but this gives a very cold and unsatisfactory meaning. It rather signifies the heart. A man when he falls into an abyss of waters, may prevent for some time the water from entering his body, by stopping his mouth and his nostrils, but at length, from its being impossible for a human being to live without respiration, suffocation will compel him to let in the waters, and they will penetrate even to the heart. David by this metaphor would intimate, not only that the waters had covered and overwhelmed him, but also that he had been forced to draw them into his body.
